Fourteen for Fourteen: The Sanctions Duel Nobody Actually Wins

On Thursday, the EU adopted its 21st sanctions package against Russia, its biggest in four years, hitting 218 individuals and entities, dozens of banks, crypto platforms, and 51 companies accused of funneling banned tech to Moscow, 14 of them Chinese or Hong Kong-based, Reuters reports. 

Brussels barely had time to enjoy the press release. Twenty-four hours later, China's Commerce Ministry answered with a mirror-image list: 14 EU entities banned from receiving Chinese dual-use goods, effective immediately.

The symmetry is the point. Beijing framed it as pure procedure, "to safeguard national security and interests, and to fulfill international obligations such as non-proliferation, in response to the E.U.'s egregious actions," a ministry spokesperson said, per ABC News. 

But look at who got hit on each side. The EU's list is mostly logistics and trading firms accused of moving banned chips. 

China's list goes straight for the jugular: German defense giant Rheinmetall, Czech military-truck maker Tatra, French drone manufacturer Cavok UAS, and a Dutch naval shipbuilder, Bloomberg reports. Fourteen against fourteen on paper. Middlemen against arms manufacturers in practice.

Polish think tank OSW calls the speed and precision of China's response "unprecedented," and notes the real target isn't this week's sanctions at all, it's the EU's planned autumn rollout of new single-market defense protections against Chinese industrial pressure, OSW's analysis explains. 

Beijing has already run this play once, quietly talking Germany out of backing tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles. Meanwhile Brussels keeps announcing record-breaking sanctions rounds while its own defense contractors discover they can't source the rare-earth magnets those sanctions were supposed to protect.

So the EU gets to call this its toughest crackdown yet, and China gets to call this just following the law, and somewhere between those two press releases, Europe's actual defense industry is the one running short on parts.

🔔 Ethereum price faces $2,000 test as oil surge revives rate fears 

⚡️ Ethereum price has remained trapped below $2,000 as rising oil prices, renewed interest-rate concerns and BitMEX’s planned shutdown have tempered bullish sentiment despite continued spot ETF inflows. According to data from cryptonews, Ethereum price traded near $1,927 on July 23 after reaching an intraday high of $1,941. The token has recovered more than 27% from its June low near $1,514, but repeated failures around $1,955 have kept the psychological $2,000 level beyond buyers’ reach.

🔗 Rate traders have already adjusted their positions. The probability of a September Fed hike rose to 79% from 68% per data from the CME FedWatch tool. Expectations for the July meeting remain centered on no change, but another oil-led inflation increase could lift Treasury yields and pressure risk assets such as Ethereum. 

🔖 U.S. equities also weakened after Alphabet raised its 2026 capital-spending forecast to between $195 billion and $205 billion. The company recorded negative free cash flow of $5.9 billion as quarterly expenditure doubled to $44.9 billion, while its shares fell in premarket trading.
